en.summary: Explains how Singapore's Chinese culture took shape through food, language, customs and everyday choices. The interactive format suits comparing local experience with Chinese culture in general, and links to collection themes such as hawker centres, dialects, festivals and family life.
en.fun_fact: The permanent exhibition uses everyday clues like local languages and food to discuss identity. The focus is how Chinese culture changed within Singapore's diverse setting, not a single-track story of ancestral origins.
en.hours: Until 30 October 2026: Mon 14:00–20:00, Tue–Sun 10:00–20:00. Closed for revamp from 31 October 2026 until end-2027.
en.price: Permanent exhibition is free
en.access_notes: This entry refers to the permanent exhibition. From 31 October 2026, do not add it to routes as a place you can enter. Check the calendar separately for other events at the centre. About 3 minutes from Shenton Way MRT Exit 3.

These reviews are of the pre-revamp version and do not reflect what will be shown after it reopens. (Listed reviews are personal experiences; small sample.)

en.summary: A gallery at the HDB headquarters in Toa Payoh that uses models, multimedia and interactive displays to explain the planning and design of public housing and community life. Good for learning how the HDB system works before observing nearby public spaces, markets and everyday neighbourhoods.
en.fun_fact: The gallery recreates Toa Payoh's classic dragon playground as an indoor exhibit, placing a generation's childhood memories within the long-term story of public housing.
en.hours: Mon–Sat 08:30–17:00; closed Sundays and public holidays. Check with HDB for ad hoc changes.
en.price: Free
en.access_notes: The gallery is in the basement of HDB Hub. Do not treat the sales show flats mentioned in older reviews as the same exhibition.
en.coordinates_note: Pin is the HDB Hub building. The gallery is in the basement; check HDB's floor plan for the entrance.
en.verification_note: 2026-10-29 is the date the online sources were checked, not a site visit date. Re-check changing details before you go.
en.review_summary: Visitors in 2019 found the city model and touch screens useful for understanding Singapore's housing development, and said students can learn from it too. Some older reviews felt the official displays were rather promotional. Reviews are old and exhibits may have changed. (Listed reviews are personal experiences; small sample.)

en.summary: A residential settlement on mainland Singapore that still keeps the look of a traditional kampong (village). Zinc roofs, dirt paths and the high-rise backdrop show the scale of the city's transformation. Suits quiet, low-impact observation and guided walks with background knowledge. It is not a theme attraction you can wander into freely.
en.fun_fact: The settlement dates from 1956. Its old name, Kampong Selak Kain, roughly means "village where you hitch up your sarong", because it flooded easily and residents lifted their clothes to wade through.
en.hours: Best visited only in daytime, briefly, along passable lanes. No set attraction opening hours.
en.price: No admission for public access areas; paid guided tours charged separately
en.access_notes: Homes and yards are private. Ask permission before photographing people or the inside of houses. Do not enter closed roads. Needs onward transport from Buangkok MRT; not a walk from the station exit.
en.coordinates_note: Checked against the location pin on public maps. Not measured on site, and not guaranteed to mark an accessible entrance.

en.routing_note: Residential settlement. Public access boundaries and tour arrangements are not confirmed, so it stays in collections but is not auto-selected for routes.
en.review_summary: 2026 reviews stress that this is still a real residential area and privacy should be respected. Earlier visitors found it small; without a guide you may only see a few houses, and a guide who knows the history adds a lot. (Listed reviews are personal experiences; small sample.)

en.summary: A historic spot in Tiong Bahru's pre-war housing estate. The exterior of the horseshoe block helps explain early public housing and wartime protection. The shelter itself is usually closed; add the exterior as a stop on a neighbourhood walk, and wait for a designated event to go inside.
en.fun_fact: Built in 1939–1940, the horseshoe block has a purpose-built air raid shelter underneath. It is one of the earliest air raid facilities specifically planned into public housing in Singapore.
en.hours: Exterior of the block can be viewed briefly in daytime; the shelter opens only for specific cultural events or approved tours
en.price: Exterior free; entry events as arranged by organisers
en.access_notes: The entrance is in the rear car park area; do not stray into residents' private spaces. Auto-generated routes can only assume an exterior visit and cannot promise access underground.
en.coordinates_note: Checked against the location pin on public maps. Not measured on site, and not guaranteed to mark an accessible entrance.

en.summary: A community gallery in Wisma Geylang Serai that uses residents' memories, objects and images to show how Geylang Serai changed from plantations to a commercial hub for the Malay community. Pairs well with a walk through the market, community buildings and nearby traditional trades.
en.fun_fact: The Geylang Serai area once had lemongrass and coconut plantations. Serai in the name means lemongrass, linking today's city streets to the farmland of the past.
en.hours: Tue–Sun 10:00–18:00. During school terms, weekdays 09:00–16:30 are mainly for school groups; public visitors must book and get confirmation.
en.price: Ask the gallery about admission and group activities
en.access_notes: Book via nhb_gshg_mbl@nhb.gov.sg. Do not assume you can walk in on term-time weekdays just because it opens at 10:00.

(Named personal visit diary; one person's experience.)

en.summary: A combined temple in the Tampines community. Good for learning how village temples merged during new town development and kept serving residents. The long dragon wall, multiple shrines and HDB backdrop mean the site tells a story of both traditional belief and urban planning.
en.fun_fact: Opened in 1992, the combined temple brings together twelve old temples, some dating to the 19th century. A dragon-shaped wall about 270 metres long holds several traditions within one complex.
en.hours: Opening hours not verified day by day; check the temple's notices before visiting
en.price: Exterior free; offerings and donations voluntary
en.access_notes: Still a community place of worship. Ask on site about opening times and rules for entering the different halls. Festivals bring more incense and crowds.

en.summary: A large place of worship in the Loyang industrial area where Taoist, Buddhist, Hindu and local guardian-spirit traditions sit side by side in one compound. Worth a dedicated trip with onward transport, especially to look at the worship spaces and how migrant cultures meet locally.
en.fun_fact: The NHB records that the main Tua Pek Kong statue survived a 1996 fire; the temple later moved to its current site. The Datuk Kong shrine on the grounds belongs to the Malayan local guardian-spirit tradition and should not simply be equated with Islamic worship.
en.hours: Official website currently lists daily 08:00–22:00, including weekends and public holidays. Not open 24 hours.
en.price: Regular visits free; offerings and donations voluntary
en.access_notes: Still needs a bus or car from Pasir Ris MRT. Respect the etiquette of each shrine. Plan your transport before leaving in the evening.

en.summary: A Sikh community centre near Balestier Road and Towner Road. Besides the prayer hall, it has a community kitchen, education and activity spaces. A respectful way to learn about Sikhism, migration history and the tradition of serving the community.
en.fun_fact: The community traces its history to an 1881 worship space for Sikh policemen. It later moved to Queen Street, then to the current site in 1986. The free vegetarian community kitchen, langar, stresses equality and service.
en.hours: Contact them first for visitor times. Prayer and community service times are not the same as free visiting hours.
en.price: No admission for regular visits; donations and service voluntary
en.access_notes: Cover your head, remove your shoes, and check with a volunteer first. Do not disturb worship or treat the community kitchen as an ordinary restaurant.

en.review_summary: A visitor in May 2026 described it as quiet and welcoming; a 2019 review advised bringing a head covering and praised the spacious prayer hall. Entry rules on site take precedence. (Listed reviews are personal experiences; small sample.)

en.summary: A traditional kampong mosque away from the main roads, keeping the religious and community memory of the old Sembawang Malay settlement. Its single-storey building, green setting and traditional timber details are very different from the dense housing estates. Best visited quietly after contacting the mosque.
en.fun_fact: The entrance still has a traditional wooden slit drum, the kentong, once used to call people to prayer. The carved central timber pillar in the prayer hall, the tiang seri, also reflects traditional Malay building methods.
en.hours: Contact them first for visitor times. Office hours (Mon–Fri 09:00–17:00, Sat 09:00–12:00) are not the same as visiting hours.
en.price: Free to view the exterior and for approved general visits
en.access_notes: Needs onward transport from the MRT. Same number for phone and WhatsApp; email admin@mpms.sg. Do not disturb prayers; ask before entering the prayer space.

en.summary: A Hindu temple where Marsiling's housing and industrial areas meet, good for exploring Indian culture in an everyday northern neighbourhood. Its main deity combines Siva and Krishna. The space is small; the painted sculptures and community activities are more interesting than looking for a big landmark.
en.fun_fact: The NHB says it is the only temple in Singapore whose main deity is the combined Siva-Krishna. In front of the shrine, Siva's bull mount and Krishna's eagle mount stand side by side.
en.hours: Normal days 06:30–12:00 and 18:00–21:00; adjusted in certain religious months
en.price: Regular visits free; offerings and donations voluntary
en.access_notes: Officially advised to take a bus from Woodlands MRT. Remove shoes inside and ask before taking photos. Older 2023 reviews mention renovation; confirm which halls are open before you go.

en.review_summary: An urban sketcher visiting in 2023 said the staff were friendly and happy to explain the deities; a 2019 visitor liked the sculptures and quiet atmosphere and felt about half an hour was enough. Earlier there was also isolated feedback unhappy with staff attitude. (Listed reviews are personal experiences; small sample.)

en.summary: Grew from a small altar set up by workers at the old Sembawang naval base and now sits in a Yishun industrial area. It links Tamil and Malayali communities with the north's shipbuilding job history, and keeps community ties through festivals, education and social aid.
en.fun_fact: "Holy Tree" refers to the tree beside the original altar. The story of dockyard workers setting up the altar in 1962 involves a religious dream tradition. The temple moved to its current site in 1996 due to redevelopment.
en.hours: Daily 07:00–12:30 and 18:00–21:00; the temple's current contact page takes precedence
en.price: Regular visits free; religious ritual services charged separately
en.access_notes: Canberra MRT is about 300 metres from the temple in a straight line, but the actual walk follows footpaths around. Closed from midday to early evening. Ask before taking photos or entering the altar area; email info@htsbt.com.sg.

The platform does not show review dates, so these cannot be taken as recent overall opinion. (Listed reviews are personal experiences; small sample.)

en.summary: A French fine-dining restaurant in Shaw Centre that turns an Orchard Road shopping trip into a refined dining experience. Dishes are based on French ingredients and classic techniques. The atmosphere is formal; set aside a full lunch or dinner slot.
en.fun_fact: The restaurant opened in 1994. Its website describes it as an early pioneer of independent fine dining in Singapore. It gained three Michelin stars in 2019 and is still on the three-star list in 2026.

en.summary: Modern French dining inside National Gallery Singapore, easy to combine with the gallery and Civic District buildings. The menu is led by Julien Royer and focuses on seasonal ingredients, precise plating and a full set-menu experience. Set aside dedicated time for the meal.
en.fun_fact: Michelin notes the restaurant was recently refreshed in warm cream tones with added banquette seating, bringing contemporary dining into the public cultural space of the former Supreme Court wing.

en.summary: A Nordic-style set-menu restaurant in a Bukit Pasoh shophouse, with seafood, Japanese influences and attentive service making up the evening. Can be combined with the historic shophouse streets on the edge of Chinatown, but booking ahead is required.
en.fun_fact: The meal is not on one floor. Michelin describes guests starting downstairs with aperitif drinks and snacks, then going upstairs for the main set menu, so the building itself shapes the order of the experience.

en.summary: A modern British restaurant on level 70 of Swissôtel The Stamford, pairing high-rise city views with British produce. Suits anniversaries and city-view themes. The view is part of the setting, but confirm your seating and menu when booking.
en.fun_fact: Michelin records how it turns British fish and chips into a refined modern dish, with a gin and tonic as a palate transition, showing how everyday food enters fine dining.

en.summary: A creative restaurant in a historic Tanjong Pagar building that links Chinese food memories with French technique. The high-ceilinged space and hanging paper artwork are distinctive. Can be combined with walking routes through Chinatown, Neil Road and Tanjong Pagar.
en.fun_fact: The building was originally the Jinrikisha Station, a rickshaw station from around 1903. A former city transport hub is now a set-menu restaurant built around the chef's life story.

en.summary: A modern Australian barbecue restaurant on Dempsey Hill. The open kitchen makes the charcoal, ovens and chefs' movements the visual focus. Pairs well with the old barracks area, galleries and green spaces of Dempsey; take a bus or short ride from Napier.
en.fun_fact: According to the restaurant group, the kitchen is built around a custom four-tonne, two-chamber oven and adjustable grills. Chef Dave Pynt shapes the dishes with wood fire rather than conventional stoves.

en.summary: A fine-dining restaurant built on Peranakan home-style flavours, good for a first proper introduction to Nonya spices, curries, buah keluak and sharing dishes. Bamboo and rattan details and the high ceilings echo Dempsey's green surroundings.
en.fun_fact: Michelin notes the chef's cooking was influenced by his mother and grandmother. The set menu presents family food memories as many small courses, with hints of Indonesian flavour.

en.summary: A creative set-menu restaurant on Amoy Street where chef Rishi Naleendra combines his Sri Lankan background, Australian experience and diverse ingredients. Can be paired with Telok Ayer's religious buildings and shophouse streets for a route from migrant history to contemporary food.
en.fun_fact: The name comes from Australian author Tim Winton's novel of the same name, a nod to the chef's training in Australia. The menu also keeps traces of Sri Lankan curry.

en.summary: A modern Korean set-menu restaurant on Mohamed Sultan Road, using seafood, vegetables and clean plating to express chef Sun Kim's food background. Can be combined with a slow walk along Robertson Quay and the Singapore River.
en.fun_fact: The website explains Meta is short for metamorphosis. The chef started out at his mother's small Korean pork bone soup shop and later worked at Tetsuya Wakuda's restaurants.

en.summary: A Cantonese restaurant in The Ritz-Carlton, Millenia Singapore, good for seeing how classic Chinese banquets, dim sum and double-boiled soups combine with modern hotel service. The room faces the gardens; pair it with Marina Centre architecture and a bayside walk.
en.fun_fact: Michelin highlights its fish bone and fish maw soup, with its milky colour and gelatinous texture, and its seafood dishes. It shows how Cantonese cooking uses slow simmering and heat control to bring out ingredients' natural flavour.

en.summary: A creative Japanese restaurant in The Shoppes at Marina Bay Sands, with a main dining room, private rooms and a chef's table. Lets you put bay views and high-end Japanese dining on the same day, but confirm the menu for each area separately.
en.fun_fact: Michelin notes the chef's table has a separate omakase menu. Its botan shrimp, sea urchin and caviar combination shows the approach of pairing Japanese ingredients with Western techniques.

en.summary: A Straits cuisine restaurant on the Gallop side of the Botanic Gardens, where the garden setting and Malcolm Lee's family food memories make for a quiet set-menu experience. Pairs well with the Gallop Extension; note the entrance is different from the main gardens.
en.fun_fact: Pangium is named after the plant that produces the buah keluak nut. This black nut is a key ingredient in Nonya cooking, and the restaurant uses the botanical name to link nature and food culture.

en.summary: A Cantonese seafood restaurant in the basement of Forum The Shopping Mall, best for group sharing meals. It keeps the ordering style of a traditional seafood restaurant within the shopping district; discuss the day's live seafood and group size with the staff.
en.fun_fact: Michelin notes the restaurant's seafood and vegetables are flown in from Hong Kong twice a week. Customers can choose how some live seafood is cooked, reflecting the Cantonese focus on ingredients and wok hei.

en.summary: A set-menu restaurant combining traditional Indian flavours with European techniques, good for exploring how Indian culture is expressed in Singapore's contemporary fine dining. Now on Mohamed Sultan Road; can be linked with the Singapore River and Fort Canning area.
en.fun_fact: The new shophouse space uses Chettinad-style details. Michelin highlights its slow-cooked spiced chicken wrapped in soft roti, linking Indian home-cooking memories with refined plating.

en.summary: A modern Singaporean restaurant at Esplanade that reworks familiar local food memories into a set menu. Best after you have eaten at hawker centres, so you can see how the chef reinterprets those flavours.
en.fun_fact: Chef LG Han starts his menu from childhood food memories. The restaurant echoes this story with local art, old photos and kitchen tools, turning the meal itself into a cultural reading.

en.summary: A contemporary restaurant in Duo Galleria whose set menu centres on the ingredients, spices and food traditions of the Malay Archipelago. Pairs with Kampong Glam, Malay culture and spice routes, with a focus on regional culture rather than a single national cuisine.
en.fun_fact: Kevin Wong founded the restaurant in 2022. Its public commitments include using seasonal vegetables and sustainable seafood, and turning trimmings into non-alcoholic drinks or artwork.

en.summary: An eight-seat sushi bar in the Keong Saik area, good for closely watching the chef prepare sushi, handle fish and season the rice. The chef is from Beijing and trained in Japan, an example of a migrant chef expressing Japanese cuisine in Singapore.
en.fun_fact: Michelin notes seafood is air-flown from Japan four times a week, and some wild bluefin tuna from Aomori is aged for extra flavour. There are only eight counter seats.

en.summary: A modern Singaporean Chinese restaurant at PARKROYAL COLLECTION Marina Bay. The menu combines Hakka, Teochew, Hokkien, Cantonese and Hainanese food with Southeast Asian life. Good for widening a Chinese food theme into the history of local migrant food.
en.fun_fact: On the new menu, per the website, Hainanese chicken rice becomes small tarts and bak kut teh is worked into a take on Buddha Jumps Over the Wall. These dishes turn familiar street flavours into a fine-dining story.
en.hours: Check the restaurant's booking calendar and same-day notices on its official website.
en.price: $$$$; à la carte and set menus

en.summary: A modern Cantonese restaurant in Capella Singapore, serving dim sum, roast meats, double-boiled soups and sharing dishes. Pairs with Sentosa's historic hotel buildings and gardens; you still need on-island transport from HarbourFront.
en.fun_fact: The website says its fish maw soup is slow-cooked for six hours with sakura chicken, dendrobium and sea whelk. Daily handmade dim sum comes with a house white peony melon tea, highlighting Cantonese slow cooking and tea culture.

en.fun_fact: Michelin records that the family has sold hand-wrapped bak chang since the 1940s; it is now run by the third generation using the family recipe, a concrete example of food craft passed down the generations.
